issues.title: Metric continuity does not make the Fréchet argmin a binary average

failure_location.quote: It is easy to verify that if the metric $d$ is continuous as a function of its arguments, then the binary Fr\'echet mean satisfies all the requirements of Definition~\ref{def:average}.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that continuity of the metric alone makes the weighted Fréchet argmin satisfy every binary-average axiom. The old paper actually establishes only the requirements in Definition~\ref{def:average}, including that the average be a single-valued map continuous in the weight; it provides no existence, uniqueness, or continuous-selection result from metric continuity. In a two-point discrete metric space the metric is continuous, but at weight $1/2$ both points minimize the objective, so the argmin is not a map. This materially defeats the claimed implication.
issues.overall_effect: The purported canonical example is not valid on a general metric space, although later convergence results that independently assume a chosen binary average are not thereby invalidated.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the claimed implication from metric continuity by the conditional statement that, for every pair and weight, the weighted Fréchet functional has a unique minimizer and that this minimizer depends continuously on the weight. Then verify the endpoint, diagonal, symmetry, and boundedness axioms by uniqueness and comparison with the two endpoints.
issues.why_classification: Metric continuity alone does not ensure existence, uniqueness, or a continuous selection, and natural metric spaces such as a two-point discrete space fail the claim. Adding well-posedness assumptions meaningfully narrows the asserted metric-space scope, so this is not a typo or lossless routine repair. The qualified Fréchet construction remains a recognizably comparable example and requires only a contained verification, so the issue is moderate rather than serious.

issues.title: Convergence results omit the finite-gap admissibility condition
issues.failure_explanation: The proof treats $C_P=\max_{0\le r<L}\delta(S^rP)$ and the resulting constant $B$ as finite, although the statement only assumes $P\in\D\subset\Omega^{\mathbb Z}$. If $\delta(P)=\infty$, the geometric majorant is infinite and supplies no $d_\infty$-Cauchy estimate. This is a real scope failure: for the linear Chaikin scheme on $\mathbb R$ with data $p_j=j^3$, the old hypotheses do not exclude the sequence, while the discrepancy between consecutive piecewise-linear interpolants is unbounded over the index at every fixed level (already the first discrepancy at the integer knot $i+1$ has magnitude $3|i+1|/4$). Hence there is no uniform convergence in the stated metric.
issues.overall_effect: The main theorem proves convergence only on finite-gap invariant domains, not for unrestricted bi-infinite sequences. General later convergence and smoothness results that inherit the unrestricted domain or invoke this theorem are likewise unestablished for infinite-gap data; results already imposing a finite bound such as $\delta(P)<1$ are unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the affected convergence results to invariant domains contained in the finite-gap sequence space, so that δ(P)<∞ and S(D)⊆D ensure every intermediate quantity in C_P is finite. Propagate this qualification through each listed dependent statement whose existing hypotheses do not already imply a finite gap; statements assuming bounds such as δ(P)<1 need no further restriction.
issues.why_classification: This repair is technically straightforward and lets the existing estimates and conclusions go through without new proof architecture. It nevertheless removes the natural and explicitly allowed class of infinite-gap bi-infinite inputs from the any-initial-data guarantees throughout the affected chain. That is a meaningful but limited scope weakening for which closely comparable finite-gap versions of all results survive, making the issue moderate.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Throughout the convergence results, we consider initial sequences \(P\) satisfying \(\delta(P)<\infty\).

issues.title: Second-type convergence theorem omits displacement safety
issues.failure_explanation: The three stated hypotheses do not imply the displacement-safe estimate used for the middle term. Concretely, on $\mathbb R$ let $M$ be the linear elementary midpoint scheme, take $L=2$, set $S_2=M$, and define $S_1(P)=-M(P)$. On the invariant domain of finite-gap sequences, $S_2$ is contractive and $S_1^2=M^2=S_2^2$, so the required block proximity is exact. Nevertheless, a nonzero constant sequence alternates between the constants $x$ and $-x$ under $S_1$ and does not converge. The scheme is not displacement-safe because its displacement on a constant sequence is nonzero while $\delta(P)=0$. Thus the unassumed premise is essential, not derivable from the other hypotheses.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised strong-convergence theorem permits uncontrolled level-to-level drift or oscillation that is invisible to block proximity. The general $C^1$ theorem inherits the same convergence gap, and the old remark denying the need for displacement safety is also invalid.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the explicit hypothesis that S1 is displacement-safe on D to the second-type convergence theorem and its dependent C1 theorem, use that estimate for the level-to-level displacement term, and revise the accompanying remark that claims displacement safety is unnecessary.
issues.why_classification: The omitted condition is used directly in the proof, and the example S1=-M shows that block proximity can coexist with persistent oscillation on every nonzero constant sequence. Thus the repair excludes a substantive class of schemes and retracts an explicit no-displacement-safety guarantee, rather than merely handling an exceptional datum. The added premise is local and leaves the proof architecture and conclusions intact for displacement-safe schemes, so the resulting weakening is moderate rather than serious.

issues.title: Second-type block proximity is iterated at the wrong scale

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In particular, note that the power of $\eta$ scales like $\cdot/L$ with respect to the number of refinements.

issues.failure_explanation: Writing $\ell=mL+r$, proximity of $S_1^L$ to $S_2^L$ can be applied to the orbit beginning at $S_1^r(P)$ and supplies an error $E_r\eta^m$. It does not supply $E\eta^{\ell-L+1}$. The old source itself notes that the power scales with the number of blocks, yet the proof iterates a fine-level exponent and consequently obtains an unjustified sum. The revised proof takes the maximum of the finitely many residue-class constants and iterates the valid block recurrence.
issues.overall_effect: For $L>1$, the displayed recurrence and the resulting decay estimate are not proved, so the general second-type convergence proof and its use in the general $C^1$ theorem are incomplete. The $L=1$ case is unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Write each level as ℓ=mL+r. For each residue r, apply block proximity to the orbit starting from S1^r(P), take the maximum E of the finitely many resulting constants, replace the fine-level error by 2Eη^m, and iterate the resulting block recurrence. Carry the same residue-class bookkeeping into the listed C1 dependency.
issues.why_classification: The erroneous exponent is used in an inference, so it is not a typo. However, the definition and the old source's own scaling remark already dictate the correction. Splitting into finitely many residue classes and reindexing the existing geometric recurrence is short, routine, and local; it introduces no new lemma or proof architecture and causes no loss of hypotheses or conclusions. The issue is therefore minor.

issues.title: Unbound level variable in first-order contractivity
issues.failure_explanation: Equation~\eqref{eqn:contractivity_diff} ends by quantifying $P\in\D$ but leaves the level $j$ in $P^j$ and in the scale factors unbound, without explicitly saying that $P^j$ ranges over every level-$j$ sequence. The proof then instantiates the condition with $S_1^{\ell-L_1}(P)$, an arbitrary level-$(\ell-L_1)$ input in $\D$. The surrounding scale convention and this invocation force the intended universal reading, which the revised definition states explicitly.
issues.overall_effect: As typeset, the $C^1$ theorem invokes an incompletely quantified hypothesis. The intended operator condition and all mathematical rates remain unchanged once the missing universal quantifier is supplied.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Bind the free level variable explicitly by stating that the first-order contractivity inequality holds for every k≥0 and every level-k sequence P^k in D, with the scales 2^{-k} and 2^{-(k+L1)}.
issues.why_classification: The displayed condition is syntactically underquantified, but its scale convention and its later application to an arbitrary level sequence uniquely force the universal operator reading. Supplying the missing quantification changes no inference, premise, rate, or guarantee, and an adept reader can make the correction directly from the old source.

issues.title: The $C^1$ theorem assumes an insufficient block-decay rate

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In particular, note that the power of $\eta$ scales like $\cdot/L$ with respect to the number of refinements.

issues.failure_explanation: If $\ell=mL_1+r$, block proximity gives a pointwise error of order $E\eta^m$. Passing to first divided differences multiplies this by $2^\ell$, yielding an error of order $2^{r+1}E(2^{L_1}\eta)^m$. The old proof instead substituted $\eta^{\ell-L_1+1}$ and obtained $(2\eta)^\ell$, although the proximity exponent counts blocks. Consequently, the proof supports the stated $C^1$ conclusion only under $2^{L_1}\eta<1$, not under the inherited condition $\eta<1/2$ for arbitrary $L_1$.
issues.overall_effect: For $L_1>1`, the theorem overstates the range of block-proximity factors for which convergence of divided differences is established. One-step applications satisfying the stronger threshold remain unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen the C1 theorem's block-proximity hypothesis to 2^{L1}η<1, equivalently η<2^{-L1}. In the proof, write ℓ=mL1+r, bound the divided-difference error by a constant times (2^{L1}η)^m, and iterate the block recurrence with β=2^{L1}η and α=max{μ1,β}.
issues.why_classification: For L1>1, the stated condition η<1/2 permits a coherent range in which multiplication by the divided-difference scale prevents the block errors from decaying. Removing that range is a substantive weakening of the advertised proximity-factor guarantee, so the issue exceeds a minor proof correction. The stronger threshold and contained recurrence repair preserve the same C1 conclusion and leave all L1=1 cases unchanged, making the issue moderate rather than serious.
